tips.title: Hierarchical is tall, flat is wide
tips.body: A **hierarchical** structure has **many layers** and a **narrow span of control**. A **flat** structure has **few layers** and a **wide span**. The same staff, arranged differently — 81 people need 5 layers at a span of 3, but only 3 at a span of 9.

tips.title: Centralised is about who decides
tips.body: **Hierarchical/flat** describes the **shape**. **Centralised/decentralised** describes **where decisions are made** — at the top, or pushed down to local managers. A business can be flat and centralised, or tall and decentralised. They are separate questions.

tips.title: Too much communication is also a problem
tips.body: The specification names **insufficient or excessive** communication. Too little causes mistakes; **too much** wastes time and buries the important message. Mentioning the excessive half is an easy mark most students miss.

tips.title: Job description describes the job
tips.body: A **job description** describes **the job** — duties and responsibilities. A **person specification** describes **the person** — skills and qualities needed. The names say which is which, so read them literally.

tips.title: Training links to retention, not just skill
tips.body: The specification asks for the **link between training, motivation and retention**. Trained staff are more capable *and* feel more valued, so they stay — which saves the cost of recruiting and training a replacement.

steps.title: Organisational structures
steps.body:
**An organisational structure sets out who reports to whom.** Two pairs of terms describe it, and they answer **different** questions.

**Hierarchical against flat — the shape.**

A **hierarchical** structure has **many layers** and a **narrow span of control** — each manager supervises few people. A **flat** structure has **few layers** and a **wide span** — each manager supervises many.

**Span of control** is how many people report directly to one manager, and it is what decides the shape. *Fernhill Garden Centres* has **81** frontline staff. At a span of **3**, the structure runs 81 → 27 → 9 → 3 → 1 — **5 layers**. At a span of **9**, it runs 81 → 9 → 1 — just **3**.

**Hierarchical**: close supervision, clear promotion ladder, defined roles. But it is **expensive** in managers, decisions travel **slowly** up and down, and messages get distorted passing through layers.

**Flat**: fewer managers so **lower costs**, **faster** communication, and staff with more responsibility. But each manager is stretched, supervision is lighter, and there are **fewer promotions** to offer.

**Centralised against decentralised — who decides.**

**Centralised**: decisions are made at the **top**. Consistent across the business, tight control, and senior experience applied everywhere — but slow, and local knowledge is wasted.

**Decentralised**: decisions are pushed **down** to local managers. Faster, responsive to local conditions, and motivating for those given the authority — but less consistent, and it relies on local managers being good.

**These are separate choices.** A business can be flat and centralised, or hierarchical and decentralised.

steps.title: Communication
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the impact of insufficient or excessive communication on efficiency and motivation.** Both directions, and both effects.

**Insufficient communication.** Staff do not know what is expected, so work is duplicated or missed and mistakes are made — **efficiency falls**. They also feel uninformed and unimportant, and hear about changes affecting them through rumour, so **motivation falls**.

**Excessive communication** is the half students forget, and it is just as real. Time spent reading messages and sitting in meetings is time not spent working, so **efficiency falls**. Worse, the message that matters is **buried** among those that do not, so important information gets missed precisely because there is so much of it. Staff who are constantly interrupted also find it harder to concentrate, which affects **motivation**.

**Barriers to effective communication:**

- **Too many layers** — the message is distorted as it passes down, which is a hierarchical structure's built-in weakness.
- **Jargon or technical language** the receiver does not understand.
- **The wrong medium** — a complex change sent by text, or a one-line fact given a meeting.
- **Physical distance**, including remote working and staff spread across sites.
- **Noise and distraction**, literal or otherwise.
- **Poor relationships**, where staff do not feel able to ask or to disagree.

**For Fernhill** the barriers are mostly structural: staff spread across several garden centres, many part-time and not present when announcements are made, and seasonal workers who were never included in the usual channels.

steps.title: Ways of working
steps.body:
**The specification covers hours, contracts and the effect of technology.**

**Hours.** **Full-time** and **part-time** are the basic split. **Flexible hours** let staff vary when they work — useful for people with caring responsibilities, and useful to the business at busy times.

**Contracts.** A **permanent** contract has no end date, giving the employee security and the business continuity and a reason to invest in training. A **temporary** contract runs for a fixed period, which suits seasonal work and lets the business adjust its costs — but the employee has no security, may be less committed, and is more likely to leave. A **freelance** worker is self-employed and paid per job: the business pays only for work done and owes no holiday or sick pay, but has less control and no guarantee the person is available next time.

**For Fernhill this is the central HR decision.** Garden centres are intensely seasonal — spring is frantic and January is quiet. **Temporary** and **part-time** contracts let it match staffing to demand instead of paying a full-time workforce through a quiet winter. The cost is that seasonal staff know less about the products, need training every year, and have little reason to be loyal.

**The impact of technology on ways of working** is framed by the specification as **efficiency** and **remote working**.

**Efficiency**: tasks are automated, information is found faster, and staff can be rostered and coordinated more precisely.

**Remote working**: people can work from anywhere. That widens the pool of applicants, cuts the need for office space and commuting, and often improves work-life balance. Against that, it makes communication harder, weakens team relationships, and makes some staff harder to supervise — and for a garden centre, most jobs cannot be done remotely at all.

steps.title: Job roles and recruitment
steps.body:
**The specification names five levels of job role.**

**Directors** set the **aims and objectives** and make the major decisions about the business as a whole.

**Senior managers** turn those objectives into plans and are responsible for large areas or departments.

**Supervisors and team leaders** oversee the day-to-day work of a small team and are the first point of contact for the people doing the job.

**Operational staff** do the work the business exists to do — serving customers, growing plants, running tills.

**Support staff** keep the business running behind that: finance, IT, human resources, administration.

**Recruitment documents.** The names say what each is, so read them literally.

- A **job description** describes **the job**: title, duties, responsibilities, who it reports to.
- A **person specification** describes **the person**: skills, qualifications, experience and qualities needed.
- An **application form** is written by the business, so every applicant answers the **same questions** and can be compared directly.
- A **CV** is written by the applicant, so it shows what **they** choose to present — and how well they present it.

**Internal recruitment** fills the post from existing staff. It is **cheaper and faster**, the person is **known** and already understands the business, and the promotion **motivates** others. But it brings **no new ideas**, and it leaves **another vacancy** to fill.

**External recruitment** brings in someone from outside: **new ideas and experience**, a **wider field** of applicants, and no gap left elsewhere. But it is **slower and more expensive**, the person is **unknown**, they need **induction**, and passing over internal candidates can **demotivate** them.

steps.title: Training and development
steps.body:
**How businesses train**, as the specification lists it:

**Formal training** is structured and planned — a course, a qualification, a scheduled session. It is thorough and can be certificated, but it costs money and takes people away from work.

**Informal training** happens on the job, by watching and being shown. It is cheap and immediately relevant, but it is inconsistent, and bad habits pass on as easily as good ones.

**Self-learning** is the employee teaching themselves — reading, online material, practice. Cheap and flexible, but it depends on motivation and there is nobody to correct a misunderstanding.

**Ongoing training for all employees** matters because training is not something done once at induction. Products, systems and rules change, and everyone needs to keep up.

**Target setting and performance reviews** are how development is directed. A review looks at how someone is doing, agrees what to improve, and sets targets to work towards before the next one.

**Why businesses train**, which is where the marks are.

**The specification asks for the link between training, motivation and retention.** Training makes staff more **capable**, so quality and productivity rise. It also makes them feel **valued** and shows a path forward, so they are **more motivated** — and motivated, capable staff are **less likely to leave**.

**Retention saves real money.** Fernhill has **120** staff. If **30** leave in a year, turnover is **25%**. After investing in training, **12** leave — turnover of **10%**, and **18 fewer people** to recruit, induct and train from scratch.

**Retraining to use new technology** is named separately. Buying equipment achieves nothing if nobody can use it — the training is part of the investment, not an optional extra.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
*Fernhill Garden Centres* has 120 staff across several sites, many part-time or seasonal. It has 81 frontline staff and 30 people left last year.

**Part A.**

1. What is meant by span of control?
2. Name the four recruitment documents.
3. Name three non-financial methods of motivation.

**Part B.**

4. Explain the difference between a hierarchical and a flat structure.
5. Calculate Fernhill's staff turnover.
6. Explain the difference between a job description and a person specification.

**Part C.**

7. Explain two problems that **excessive** communication could cause at Fernhill.
8. Explain why Fernhill uses temporary contracts, and one drawback of doing so.
9. Recommend how Fernhill could reduce its staff turnover, and justify your answer.

For question 9, remember its margins are thin — a large pay rise may not be available.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep the two pairs of terms apart.** **Hierarchical/flat** is the **shape**; **centralised/decentralised** is **who decides**. They are independent, and a business can be flat and centralised. Treating them as the same pair is a common and costly confusion.

**Use the span of control to explain the shape.** A narrow span means **more layers** for the same staff — 81 people need 5 layers at a span of 3 but only 3 at a span of 9. That single comparison explains why hierarchical structures cost more in managers and communicate more slowly.

**Mention excessive communication.** The specification says **insufficient or excessive**, and almost every answer covers only the first. Too much communication **buries** the important message and consumes working time — an easy mark sitting unclaimed.

**Read the recruitment documents literally.** The **job description** describes the **job**; the **person specification** describes the **person**. Note also who writes what: the **application form** is the business's, so candidates can be compared on the same questions; the **CV** is the candidate's, so it shows what they choose to present.

**Link training to retention, not just to skill.** The specification asks for the link between **training, motivation and retention**. Trained staff are more capable **and** feel more valued, so fewer leave — and each leaver avoided saves recruiting, inducting and training a replacement. Cutting turnover from 25% to 10% is 18 fewer replacements a year.

**Explain why non-financial methods often work better.** A pay rise is quickly absorbed into what feels normal, and it must be paid again every year. **Autonomy**, **job enrichment** and **job rotation** cost little and do not wear off in the same way. For a business with thin margins this is the practical answer, not a second-best one.

**Apply it to the business.** A garden centre is **seasonal**, so **temporary** and **part-time** contracts match staffing to demand — and the cost is staff who know the products less well and have little reason to be loyal. That is application, and it is what the levels reward.

**Judge, and say what it depends on.** *Fernhill should use non-financial methods because its margins cannot support a pay rise, provided pay is already at the market rate* is a conclusion. If pay is **below** the market rate, no amount of job enrichment will fix it — and saying so shows real judgement.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Span of control** is how many report directly to one manager.
- **Hierarchical**: many layers, narrow span — costly, slower, more promotion rungs.
- **Flat**: few layers, wide span — cheaper, faster, fewer promotions.
- 81 staff need **5 layers** at a span of 3, but **3** at a span of 9.
- **Centralised**: decisions at the top. **Decentralised**: decisions pushed down.
- Shape and decision-making are **separate** choices.
- **Insufficient** communication causes mistakes and makes staff feel unvalued.
- **Excessive** communication wastes time and **buries** what matters.
- Barriers: too many layers, jargon, the wrong medium, distance, noise, poor relationships.
- Contracts: **permanent**, **temporary**, **freelance**; hours: full-time, part-time, **flexible**.
- Technology affects **efficiency** and enables **remote working**.
- Roles: **directors, senior managers, supervisors, operational staff, support staff**.
- **Job description** describes the job; **person specification** describes the person.
- **Internal** recruitment is cheaper and known; **external** brings new ideas.
- Motivation matters for **attracting**, **retaining** and **productivity**.
- **Financial**: remuneration, bonus, commission, promotion, fringe benefits. **Non-financial**: job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy.

questions.prompt: A business with 120 staff cuts leavers from 30 to 12 a year. By how many percentage points does its staff turnover fall?
questions.solution: Before: $(30 \div 120) \times 100 = 25\%$. After: $(12 \div 120) \times 100 = 10\%$. The fall is **15 percentage points**, which is 18 fewer people to recruit, induct and train.

Non-financial methods are legally required for small businesses
Employees prefer not to be paid more than the minimum wage
Financial methods cannot be used alongside training
questions.solution: **Autonomy**, **job enrichment** and **job rotation** cost almost nothing, which matters when margins are thin. A pay rise is also quickly absorbed into what feels normal and must be paid again every year, whereas interesting work and real responsibility do not wear off the same way.

questions.solution: With each manager supervising few people, more managers are needed — and more **layers** of them. Covering 81 staff at a span of 3 takes **five** layers, against **three** at a span of 9, and every extra manager is a salary.

questions.solution: Internal recruitment is cheaper, faster and motivating, but it only reshuffles people who already think the way the business thinks. Over time that means **no fresh ideas or outside experience**, and it also leaves **another vacancy** each time.

questions.prompt: Fernhill Garden Centres employs 120 staff across several sites, many part-time or on temporary seasonal contracts. Last year 30 staff left. Its profit margins are thin. Analyse how Fernhill could reduce its staff turnover.
questions.solution:
Fernhill's staff turnover is $(30 \div 120) \times 100 = \textbf{25\%}$ — one worker in four leaving each year. That is costly: every leaver must be **recruited, inducted and trained**, and during the weeks before a replacement is useful the remaining staff carry the work.

**The causes are visible in how the business is organised.** Much of the workforce is **temporary and seasonal**, and a temporary contract offers no security and little reason to be loyal, so some of that 25% is designed into the staffing model rather than being a failure of management. The business is also **multi-site** and heavily **part-time**, so staff may feel disconnected — part-time workers are often absent when announcements are made and can end up outside the normal channels of communication altogether.

**Training is the strongest lever available.** The specification links **training, motivation and retention** directly: trained staff are more **capable**, so the work goes better, and they feel **valued** and can see a path forward, so they are more likely to stay. For a garden centre this is doubly useful, because plant knowledge is exactly what customers come in for — so the training that keeps staff also improves the service.

**Non-financial motivation suits this business particularly well** because its **margins are thin**. **Autonomy** — letting experienced staff choose planting displays or reorganise their section — costs nothing and gives real ownership of the work. **Job enrichment** and **job rotation** add variety and challenge, which matters in a role that could otherwise be repetitive. These methods are cheap, and their effect does not wear off the way a pay rise does once it becomes the new normal.

**Better communication would also help.** With staff across several sites and many working part-time, it is easy for people to feel peripheral. Making sure part-time and seasonal staff are actually included — not merely sent messages — addresses the sense of being an afterthought that drives people out.

The chain worth following is this: better training and more autonomy → staff feel more capable and valued → **fewer leave** → turnover falls from 25% towards, say, 10%, which is **18 fewer people to replace each year** → recruitment and training costs fall, and the staff who remain know the products better → **better customer service** → more repeat custom and higher revenue. The saving is not only the recruitment cost; it is the expertise that stops walking out of the door.

**Judgement.** Fernhill should focus on **training and non-financial motivation**, because they fit both its financial position and the nature of the work. But this depends on **pay already being near the market rate**: if Fernhill pays less than the garden centre down the road, no amount of job enrichment will hold staff, and the pay must be fixed first.

It should also accept that **some turnover is unavoidable and even appropriate**. Seasonal contracts exist because demand is seasonal, and students and temporary workers will always move on. The realistic target is to retain the **permanent, knowledgeable core** — not to drive 25% to zero, which would mean abandoning the flexible staffing that makes a seasonal business affordable at all.

questions.prompt: Fernhill Garden Centres has 81 frontline staff and is considering moving from a hierarchical structure with a span of control of 3 to a flatter structure with a span of 9, and decentralising decisions to individual site managers. Evaluate whether Fernhill should make these changes.
questions.solution:
These are **two separate changes**, and it is worth treating them separately because a business can adopt either without the other. The **shape** of the structure and **who makes decisions** are independent questions.

**The change in shape.** With **81** frontline staff and a span of control of **3**, the structure runs 81 → 27 → 9 → 3 → 1, which is **five layers**. Widening the span to **9** gives 81 → 9 → 1 — just **three layers**.

The immediate saving is in **managers**. Two entire layers of management disappear, and each of those posts is a salary, so the wage bill falls appreciably. For a business described as having **thin margins**, that is a substantial and permanent reduction in fixed costs.

**Communication should also improve.** A message currently passes through five layers between the top and the shop floor, and is distorted a little at each one — the specification names too many layers as a barrier to effective communication. With three layers, instructions arrive faster and more accurately, and information travels back up more readily too.

**The costs of flattening.** Each manager would supervise **nine** people rather than three, which is far less individual attention. New and seasonal staff — of whom Fernhill has many — need more supervision than experienced ones, so a wide span is hardest precisely where this business is weakest. Overstretched managers also make poorer decisions and are themselves at risk of leaving.

There are **fewer promotions** too. Removing two layers removes two rungs of the ladder, and promotion is one of the financial motivators the specification names. For a business already losing **25%** of its staff a year, reducing the visible ways to progress works against retention at exactly the wrong moment.

**Decentralising decisions** is the stronger of the two proposals for this particular business. Fernhill operates across **several sites**, and a garden centre's trade depends on **local conditions** — the weather, the soil, what sells in that area, when the local schools break up. A site manager can respond to those far faster than a head office can. Decentralising also **motivates** the managers themselves, since **autonomy** is a non-financial motivator and a powerful one.

The risks are **inconsistency** between sites and dependence on the **quality of each site manager**. If one manager makes poor buying decisions, head office may not notice until the stock is unsold. A business with high turnover may also have site managers who are relatively new to the role.

**Conclusion.** Fernhill should **decentralise, and flatten more cautiously**.

Decentralising fits the business almost perfectly: it is multi-site, it is seasonal, its trade is local, and the change costs nothing while motivating the managers it affects. The risks are real but manageable through clear limits on what site managers may decide and regular reporting back.

Flattening from five layers to three in one step is more than this business should take on at once. The cost saving is attractive, but a span of **nine** over a largely part-time and seasonal workforce risks supervision failing where it is most needed, and removing promotion rungs while turnover is already at 25% could make that worse. Removing **one** layer rather than two would capture much of the saving and the faster communication while leaving spans manageable.

What the decision ultimately depends on is the **experience of the staff being supervised**. If Fernhill's frontline is mostly long-serving and knowledgeable, a wide span is perfectly workable. If it is largely seasonal and new each spring — which the 25% turnover suggests — then close supervision is doing necessary work, and removing it to save management salaries would cost more in service quality and mistakes than it saves in wages.

examTechnique.body:
Keep **hierarchical/flat** (the shape) apart from **centralised/decentralised** (who decides) — they are independent. Use the **span of control** to explain why a structure has the layers it does.

Cover **excessive** as well as insufficient communication. Link **training to retention**, not just to skill, and apply every point to the **business in the question**.
examinerErrors: Treating flat and decentralised as the same thing.
Describing layers without mentioning the span of control.
Covering only insufficient communication and not excessive.
Swapping the job description and the person specification.
Linking training to skill alone, not to motivation and retention.
Recommending a pay rise without considering what the business can afford.
Giving generic HR points with no reference to the business in the question.
Ending with "there are advantages and disadvantages" and no judgement.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates the **shape** of a structure from **who makes the decisions**, and uses the **span of control** to show why — 81 staff need five layers at a span of 3 but three at a span of 9. It covers **excessive** communication as well as insufficient, and links **training to motivation and retention** with a figure attached. It chooses motivation methods the business can actually **afford**, noting that non-financial methods are cheap and do not wear off. Every point names the business — **seasonal**, **multi-site**, **part-time** — and it closes with a **judgement that names what it depends on**, such as whether pay is already at the market rate.
